claims.text: The starting material is a single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents.
The carbon-containing alloy is rapidly consolidated by U-FAST and then subjected to a short subcritical anneal.
Carbon addition and the specified processing will form fine or nanoscale titanium-carbide precipitates along grain boundaries.
The titanium-carbide precipitates will pin grain boundaries and inhibit grain coarsening during high-temperature exposure.
Inhibiting grain coarsening will limit diffusion-mediated softening.
Long-term exposure near 1000°C can produce grain growth accompanied by a decrease in hardness in a U-FAST-processed titanium-containing high-entropy alloy.
The carbon-doped alloy will have less grain growth than the carbon-free processed control during elevated-temperature exposure.
The carbon-doped alloy will retain higher microhardness than the carbon-free processed control.
The carbon-doped alloy will retain greater bulk strength than the carbon-free processed control at elevated temperature.
The proposed testing range is 800–1100°C in an inert atmosphere, with exposure durations up to 1000 hours.
The hypothesis applies while the alloy maintains a single-phase solid-solution microstructural framework.
Carbon may form undesirable secondary phases outside the optimal processing window.
The optimal carbon content and carbide-precipitation processing parameters have not been established.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvement in grain-size stability, hardness retention, or high-temperature strength relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary requires maintenance of a single-phase solid solution, whereas the intervention is explicitly intended to form titanium-carbide precipitates, creating an additional phase.
